newsitem.title: UK: Sterling soars as U.K. inflation pressures grow.
newsitem.headline: Sterling soars as U.K. inflation pressures grow.

text.p: Sterling soared on Tuesday after an unexpectedly strong rise in British inflation made investors even more certain of another rise in interest rates this week.

The underlying rate of price inflation jumped above the government's 2.5 percent target, hitting 2.7 percent in June. The headline inflation rate, which includes mortgage payments, rose to 2.9 percent from 2.6 in May.
It was the highest figure for headline inflation since January 1996.
Shares fell on the gloomy inflation news and the price of government bonds also dropped.
The strong pound, which is already hurting British exporters, jumped to a new six-year high over 2.97 German marks, up over three pfennigs from late prices seen in Europe.
It eased back only a shade on vague rumours of Bank of England selling in the foreign currency markets.
Sterling rallied to near seven month highs against the dollar, rising to 1.6930 dollars from 1.6850 late on Monday.
The rise was powered by market talk of a half point rise in British interest rates from the newly-independent Bank of England which starts its monthly meeting on Wednesday.
However, some economists were more sanguine, pointing to the one-off impact of strong food price rises, sent higher by the wet weather in June.
Most analysts see a quarter point rise in rates, continuing the recent trend for small rate adjustments. A statement from the Bank of England is due at midday on Thursday.
Nigel Richardson, head of bond research at Yamaichi International Europe, said comfort could be drawn from the impact of food prices in last month's inflation figures.
But he added, "The underlying tone from this set of data is obviously disappointing and does point in a direction of a rate rise."
Interest rates have already risen three times since last October and speculation of another rise intensified after last week's budget from the new Labour government.
The budget raised the tax burden by around six billion pounds, but most of the measures hit business and did little to restrain sharply rising consumer demand.

A consumer boom fuelled partly by windfall payouts from demutualised building societies as well as rising wages is risking an inflation push that is only being masked by the anti-inflationary impact of the strong British pound.
But inflation risks taking off as soon as the pound starts easing, which could happen once interest rates are believed to have peaked.
In the short-run, however, exporters are expecting more pain from a pound which many in the market say could be on its way up to three marks after the next interest rate increase.
The impact is already being felt, with new figures out on Tuesday showing second quarter export orders from British engineering firms at their lowest level in three years.

British stocks reacted badly to the inflation news, with the FTSE 100 share index down 32 points or 0.7 percent by midday at just below 4,780. It had been at a new record high of 4879.0 just days ago.
Government bond prices remained generally lower with the September gilt contract trading down 7/32 at 114-19/32.
